items.title: The Christian Science Monitor Daily for October 22, 2026
items.excerpt: ## News briefs Russia agreed to resume three-way talks on the Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington. A Kremlin official said Wednesday that negotiations with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine are set to resume after Nov. 10 and will focus on building a security system for Russia and Ukraine. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday in St. Petersburg for about three hours. A day earlier, Mr. Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in the Norwegian capital of Oslo, suggesting renewed momentum in peace efforts. – Associated Press Our coverage: With US and Ukraine at odds, Russia cautiously tries to take advantage Iran says 7 tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. This happened overnight Thursday, possibly marking the largest single-day incident since the Iran war began on February 28. Four tankers caught fire after being targeted, while three others were immobilized by naval mines. The report warns that the Revolutionary Guard may target U.S. bases if the U.S. tries to allow tankers to transit through other parts of the strait. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia reports two deaths from an attack on King Fahd International Airport. – AP Britain approved new gas drilling in the North Sea. After years of legal and political wrangling the Labour government gave the green light to the Jackdaw gas field, saying it would help ease energy costs that have surged during the Iran war. It will begin supplying gas by the end of this month. The Green Party called the approval “climate vandalism” but Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said it was compatible with Britain’s target of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050. The Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from restricting gender affirming care in federal prisons. The decision, announced in a one-sentence order on Wednesday, upholds a lower court ruling. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would have granted the administration’s request to stay the lower court ruling while the case is pending a final decision. The case will now proceed in federal district court in Washington, D.C. Approximately 1,000 transgender federal inmates are challenging the policy. Our coverage: Lifesaving or harmful? Trans care debate barrels toward 2024. Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard. Mr. Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff announced the release Wednesday during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg. The United States government under the Biden administration designated Mr. Hubbard as wrongfully detained. The release comes as President Donald Trump advances policies that aid Mr. Putin, including waiving sanctions on Russia. – AP Tiny Caribbean island to restore Alexander Hamilton museum with U.S. funds. The island of Nevis has received a financial boost in honor of one of its most famous sons, Alexander Hamilton, who went on to become a founding father of the United States and America’s first treasury secretary. The U.S. government this month awarded $245,000 to restore the home where some believe Hamilton once lived. Hamilton spent his childhood on Nevis at his adopted father’s home in Charlestown. The building is now Hamilton House, a museum that houses documents from his early years. – AP

items.title: Early Edition: October 22, 2026
items.excerpt: A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news: IRAN WAR Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy today said four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by Iranian forces yesterday. The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the U.S. military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. Tala Ramadan reports for Reuters. The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterms, U.S. officials and other sources told the New York Times. The countries’ militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. The strikes would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Julian E. Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Farnaz Fassihi, Natan Odenheimer, and Ronen Bergman report. Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets on Monday conducted a sortie, flying as far as the Iranian border, Israeli and U.S. officials told Axios. The operation took place on the same day U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but wasn’t connected to Hegseth’s visit. Barak Ravid reports. IRAN WAR – YEMEN Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation yesterday blamed the Iran-aligned Houthis for a new attack on the eastern Saudi city of Dammam’s airport which killed two people and injured another eight. The U.S. State Department said it ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families from the kingdom in response to increased hostilities against Saudi Arabia by the Houthis. David Gritten reports for BBC News; James T. Areddy and Abeer Ayyoub report for the Wall Street Journal. IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS ... New York Democrat congressional candidate Brad Lander yesterday said he was briefly detained and released by the Israeli military while he was supporting Palestinian farmers during an olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. The New Israel Fund said approximately 90 volunteers of what they’re calling the Protect the Harvest initiative were released. Two Israeli lawyers told NPR it was the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West Bank in at least a decade. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said Lander’s actions amounted to “political provocation,” and noted that he chose to enter a restricted area and participate in an unauthorized activity without coordinating with local authorities. Joseph De Avila reports for the Wall Street Journal; Ruth Sherlock, Samantha Balaban, Nuha Musleh, and Daniel Estrin report. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff yesterday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” following the release of U.S. citizen Stephen James Hubbard from Russian custody. In a meeting between the pair, Putin told Witkoff that he “agrees in principle” to resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States to end the war in Ukraine, Russian and U.S. officials told Axios. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he hoped the three-way talks will be held as soon as possible, preferably no later than early November. David E. Sanger, Kim Barker, and Ivan Nechepurenko ... The U.N. World Meteorological Organization yesterday said the El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels across the world like a “wrecking ball,” causing floods and droughts. The WMO’s seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong and cause temperatures to rise by 3.8 degrees Celsius. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said “we have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around 3 in some record El Niños before, with very substantive impacts across the world.” Olivia Le Poidevin reports for Reuters. ... Solicitor General D. John Sauer yesterday submitted an emergency application to the Supreme Court to allow the Trump administration to move forward with construction of a border wall along hundreds of miles in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas. A federal judge blocked construction of the barriers which had drawn local objections. Sauer called the lower court “baseless” and asserted that halting the section of the wall at issue would leave “a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses.” Abbie VanSickle reports for the New York Times.

items.title: IIF Global Macro Views: What the Breadth of U.S. Inflation Signals > The Institute of International Finance
items.excerpt: - Broad inflation is the Fed’s challenge; entrenchment is the risk. Prices are rising across much of the U.S. economy, but softer momentum and weaker hiring complicate the case for further tightening. - The latest price shock is being transmitted through production costs. Energy pushed September CPI and PPI higher, while measures of underlying inflation rose more moderately. - Households are more alarmed about inflation than bond investors. Fuel prices shift near-term expectations quickly; evidence that breadth changes longer-term beliefs is less conclusive. - Monetary policy is the clearest link to bond yields. Persistent breadth could raise the expected policy path, although real yields also respond to fiscal, investment, and global forces.

items.title: U.S. Inflation Rises 3.7% As Economists See December Fed Hike | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year through September, while a Reuters poll found all 100 economists surveyed expected a December Federal Reserve rate increase. September’s price data showed gasoline rising 34.2% year over year, while the Federal Reserve has not yet made its October decision. A measure excluding food and energy increased 2.6%. The energy index gained 20.4%, with gasoline prices up 34.2% over the same 12-month period. ... Reuters said its Oct. 16-20 survey found 94 economists expected no change to the Fed’s 3.75%-4.00% target range at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. All 100 respondents projected a rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. EconoTimes previously covered the survey’s unanimous December outlook. In responses about the rate’s eventual peak, nearly 60% expected a range of 4.00%-4.25%; 38 of 92 respondents anticipated at least two more increases. The Fed’s September move lifted its target range by 0.25 percentage point in a unanimous 12-0 vote, setting it at 3.75%-4.00%. Reuters also reported that Michael Gapen, Morgan Stanley’s chief U.S. economist, saw risks pointing to the Fed needing to raise rates more than Morgan Stanley expected.

items.title: US inflation rose slightly last month after 2 years of steady cooling but remained low
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — Inflation in the United States ticked up in October, driven by costlier rents, used cars and air fares, a sign that price increases might be leveling off after having slowed in September to their lowest pace since 2021. Consumer prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 2.4% in September. It was the first rise in annual inflation in seven months. From September to October, prices edged up 0.2%, the same as the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, “core” prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, the same as in September. From September to October, core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Over the long run, core inflation at that pace would exceed the Fed’s 2% target. ... An uptick in prices, if sustained, could stir concerns in financial markets that progress in taming inflation may be slowing. It might also make the Federal Reserve less inclined to cut its key interest rate in the coming months, as its officials have previously indicated they likely would. ... Still, most economists think inflation will eventually resume its slowdown. Consumer inflation, which peaked at 9.1% in 2022, has since fallen steadily, though overall prices are still about 20% higher than they were three years ago. ... In addition, the economy is growing faster than many economists had expected earlier this year. It has expanded at nearly a 3% annual rate over the past six months, with consumers, particularly those with higher incomes, spending freely and fueling growth. ... A survey released Tuesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that consumers expect prices to rise just 2.9% in the next 12 months, which would be the lowest such measure in nearly four years. Lower inflation expectations are important because when consumers expect milder price increases, they’re less likely to act in ways that raise inflation, such as accelerating their purchases or demanding higher pay to offset higher prices. ... Another potential source of relief for Americans’ budgets is in apartment rents. They are now barely rising on average nationwide, according to the real estate brokerage Redfin. Its measure of median rent was just 0.2% higher than it was a year ago in October, at $1,619, though that figure reflects rents only for new leases.
